notes: MD 2000 places the PCT in slot 5; as the ruling party of 1970 (founded 29-31 Dec 1969, chaired by Ngouabi) it must sit in ruling slot 4. Pre-1963 parties (UDDIA, MSA, PPC) are banned since the single-party law and appear as underground/exile networks. Slot 18 holds Massamba-Débat's dissolved MNR.

0.name: Union démocratique de défense des intérêts africains
0.english: Democratic Union for the Defence of African Interests
0.native_full: Union démocratique de défense des intérêts africains
0.text:
The UDDIA was the ruling party of Abbé Fulbert Youlou, the defrocked priest who led Congo to independence and was toppled by the Trois Glorieuses rising of August 1963. Banned ever since, it survives as a clandestine network among the Lari of the Pool, while Youlou lives in exile in Madrid.

Youlouists stand for close ties with France and the West, a free economy, the Church and hostility to the 'scientific socialism' of Brazzaville. Their leverage lies in Lari loyalty in the Pool and in sympathisers across the river in Kinshasa, where Mobutu tolerates Congolese exiles hostile to Ngouabi.
0.wiki: Democratic Union for the Defence of African Interests

1.name: Archidiocèse de Brazzaville
1.text:
The Catholic Church is the largest organised body in Congo outside the state, with schools, seminaries and parishes reaching deep into the south. Archbishop Théophile Mbemba, the first Congolese to lead the see, heads it in 1970, after the nationalisation of Church schools in 1965 cost it much of its influence.

The Church defends religious education, the family and private property against Marxist-Leninist doctrine, and quietly favours links with France and Rome. Its leverage rests on a large, devout southern laity and on clergy who still speak with moral authority the regime cannot easily silence.

2.name: Parti progressiste congolais
2.text:
The PPC was founded in 1946 by Jean-Félix Tchicaya, Congo's first deputy in the French National Assembly and the political voice of the Vili of Pointe-Noire. Weakened after Tchicaya's death in 1961 and banned under the single-party system, it lives on as a network of coastal notables and civil servants.

Its heirs favour constitutional government, regional balance, an open port economy and cooperation with France. Their influence rests on the Vili elite of the Kouilou, on Pointe-Noire's merchants and dockers, and on the prestige of the Tchicaya name in a coast that resents Brazzaville's dominance.

3.name: Mouvement socialiste africain
3.text:
The MSA was the Congolese section of the French SFIO's African network, led by Jacques Opangault, the Mbochi politician who rivalled Youlou in the 1950s. Absorbed into the single party in 1963 and banned as an independent force, it persists as a circle of older northern politicians and teachers around Opangault.

It stands for democratic socialism, trade-union rights, parliamentary government and a moderate foreign policy linked to European socialists rather than Moscow. Its base lies among northern civil servants and teachers, and its standing as the historic party of the north gives it a hearing within Ngouabi's own milieu.

4.name: Parti congolais du travail
4.text:
The PCT was founded at its constituent congress of 29-31 December 1969 as Africa's first self-declared Marxist-Leninist vanguard party, replacing the National Council of the Revolution. Commandant Marien Ngouabi chairs its Central Committee and is head of state, proclaiming the People's Republic of the Congo with a red flag and the Internationale.

The party pursues scientific socialism: nationalised key sectors, cadres trained in Moscow, Havana and East Berlin, and close ties with the Soviet bloc and China while French oil and timber companies keep operating. Its power rests on the army, a small urban cadre and northern officers loyal to Ngouabi.

5.name: Union générale des élèves et étudiants congolais
5.english: General Union of Congolese Pupils and Students
5.native_full: Union générale des élèves et étudiants congolais
5.text:
The UGEEC organises Congo's lycée and university students and is the most radical voice in Brazzaville's politics. Shaped by May 1968 in Paris, the Black Power movement and the Cultural Revolution, its militants mock the PCT as a barracks party and demand a genuine revolution from below.

It calls for the purge of 'bureaucratic bourgeois' officials, total nationalisation, the end of French military and economic presence and a people's militia instead of a professional army. Its leverage lies in strikes and street demonstrations, and in sympathisers among young political commissars such as Ange Diawara.

6.name: Défense civile
6.text:
The Défense civile was the armed militia of the National Movement of the Revolution, trained with Cuban help after 1965 as a counterweight to the regular army. Defeated at Camp Biafra in 1968 and disarmed by Ngouabi's paratroopers, its veterans remain a resentful hardline current inside the youth movement and party.

They stand for an uncompromising revolutionary order: armed workers' militias, ruthless repression of 'counter-revolutionaries', rigid party discipline and an alliance with Cuba and the Soviet bloc. Their leverage lies in hidden weapons, militant youth in Bacongo and Makélékélé, and old comrades still placed in the security services.

7.name: Les Officiers du Nord
7.text:
Behind the PCT's revolutionary language stands a tight bloc of northern officers, mostly Mbochi and Kouyou, who seized control of the army in 1968 and carried Marien Ngouabi to power. Men such as chief of staff Joachim Yhombi-Opango and the paratrooper officer Denis Sassou Nguesso form its core.

The bloc values order, command and the security apparatus over doctrine, using Marxist-Leninist rhetoric and Soviet arms to secure northern dominance over a state long run by southerners. Its leverage is decisive: it controls the paratroop battalion, the gendarmerie and the intelligence services that keep the regime alive.

8.name: Les Négociants libanais de Pointe-Noire
8.text:
A small Lebanese community, largely Shia families from Jabal Amil, runs shops, import houses and transport firms in Pointe-Noire and Brazzaville. Its notables follow the revival led in Lebanon by Imam Musa al-Sadr, whose Supreme Islamic Shia Council was founded in 1969.

The merchants favour a modern, socially engaged Shia identity, education for their children and quiet accommodation with whoever rules Congo. Their influence comes from money rather than numbers: credit, import licences and trade networks the nationalising regime still needs, and links to the wider Lebanese diaspora in West and Central Africa.

9.name: Les Fidèles de Najaf
9.text:
A handful of young Lebanese Shia in Congo, schooled in religious seminaries in South Lebanon and in contact with students of the Najaf hawza, form a devout circle around their community's prayer gatherings. They reject both the secular Marxism of the PCT and the assimilated commerce of their elders.

They look to the clerical scholars of Najaf for guidance, preach strict observance and clerical authority, and condemn Western and Soviet materialism alike. Their numbers are tiny, but they carry weight in family councils and among the poorer shop assistants of the Lebanese diaspora.

10.name: Les Imams de Poto-Poto
10.text:
Poto-Poto, Brazzaville's cosmopolitan quarter, is home to the city's Muslims: Senegalese, Malian, Hausa and Guinean traders whose families settled in the colonial era. Their imams and elders lead the mosques of the quarter and settle disputes within the community.

They practise a conservative Maliki Sunni Islam, keep away from politics and seek good relations with any government that protects their trade and worship. Their leverage lies in commerce: West African traders dominate parts of Brazzaville's retail trade, and pilgrim contacts with Saudi Arabia and the Muslim World League bring modest funding.

11.name: Le Cercle de la Hijra
11.text:
Among returning pilgrims and Hausa traders in Poto-Poto, a small circle preaches that Muslims cannot live under an atheist state. It draws on the memory of Usman dan Fodio's jihad and of Mahdist movements across the Sahel, and gathers in private homes rather than in the official mosques.

It rejects both communism and Western secularism, calls for a community governed solely by sharia and dreams of a restored caliphate uniting Africa's Muslims. It has no arms and few followers, but its message resonates with young traders angered by the regime's hostility to religion.

12.name: Les Anciens d'Al-Azhar
12.text:
A few young Congolese and West African Muslims have returned from scholarships at Al-Azhar in Cairo, where they encountered the ideas of the Muslim Brotherhood despite Nasser's repression. They teach in Qur'anic schools in Poto-Poto and in the small Muslim communities of Pointe-Noire and the north.

They promote modern Islamic education, Arabic literacy, moral renewal and organised welfare, presenting Islam as an answer to both colonial Christianity and Marxism. Their influence rests on the classroom and the community association rather than politics, giving them a foothold among educated Muslim youth.

13.name: Le Cercle des technocrates
13.text:
Around Major Alfred Raoul, the polytechnic-trained officer who served as prime minister and interim head of state in 1968-1969, gathers a circle of engineers, planners and senior civil servants. They run the ministries, the state enterprises and the Congo-Ocean Railway while ideologues debate doctrine.

The technocrats want a strong, competent state, planned development and pragmatic dealings with France, the Soviet bloc and international lenders alike. They care little for Marxist slogans, and their leverage lies in expertise the regime cannot replace and in Raoul's standing as a moderate within the ruling council.

14.name: Matsouanisme
14.native_full: Amicale des originaires de l'Afrique-Équatoriale française
14.text:
The Matswa movement grew from the Amicale founded in 1926 by André Grenard Matswa, a Lari veteran who died in French custody in 1942. His followers came to venerate him as a messiah and still refuse taxes, identity cards and voting, awaiting his return in the villages of the Pool.

Matsouanists defend Lari and Kongo customs, the authority of elders and spiritual independence from every state, colonial or revolutionary. They distrust Marxism as much as Youlou once did. Their leverage is passive resistance: entire communities refuse cooperation, and their devotion makes the Pool region ungovernable by force alone.

15.name: Chambre de commerce de Pointe-Noire
15.native_full: Chambre de commerce, d'agriculture et d'industrie de Pointe-Noire
15.text:
The Pointe-Noire Chamber of Commerce brings together the French trading houses, timber companies, shipping agents and oil interests of Congo's only deep-water port. Its members handle the okoumé and limba exports, the Gabonese manganese moved by rail and the first offshore oil prospecting.

The chamber defends private property, the franc zone and French investment against nationalisation, preferring discreet bargaining to open politics. Its leverage is economic: the port, the railway and foreign trade generate most of the state's revenue, and the regime cannot afford to drive out the companies that keep them running.

16.name: Les Commerçants du Marché Total
16.english: The Traders of the Marché Total
16.text:
The Marché Total in Bacongo is Brazzaville's great market, where Lari market women, tailors, taxi owners and small wholesalers run a vigorous private economy. Price controls, state trading companies and party inspectors have made them the regime's most persistent everyday critics.

They want free prices, low taxes, an end to state monopolies and the right to trade across the river with Kinshasa without harassment. They have no party, but their leverage is real: they feed the capital, and a closed market or a hoarding wave can bring Brazzaville to its knees within days.

17.name: Service des Eaux et Forêts
17.text:
The Water and Forests Service, inherited from the colonial administration, manages Congo's vast rainforests and the Odzala reserve established in 1935. Its foresters, many trained in France, watch the timber companies push ever deeper into the forests of the Kouilou, Niari and Sangha.

Its officers argue for sustainable logging quotas, reforestation, protection of elephants and gorillas and control of the bushmeat trade. They lack political weight but hold technical authority over concessions, and their reports give the state a lever to restrain foreign timber firms when it chooses to use it.

18.name: Mouvement national de la révolution
18.text:
The MNR was Congo's single party from 1964 under President Alphonse Massamba-Débat, who proclaimed a 'Bantu socialism' and opened relations with China and Cuba. Pushed aside by the army in 1968 and superseded by the PCT, its leaders are sidelined and Massamba-Débat lives in retirement in his native Boko.

Its heirs favour a humanist, African socialism rooted in cooperatives, education and non-alignment rather than Soviet-style Leninism, and civilian rather than military rule. Their leverage lies in southern civil servants, teachers and the Lari and Kongo populations who still regard Massamba-Débat as the legitimate president.

19.name: La Ligne de Pékin
19.text:
Congo has been one of China's closest partners in Africa since 1964, and Chinese aid, textiles and Little Red Books circulate widely in Brazzaville. Within the PCT and the army's political commissariat, a radical wing led by the young commissar Ange Diawara admires the Cultural Revolution.

It calls for a mass line, the mobilisation of peasants, the purge of the 'bureaucratic bourgeoisie' and independence from Soviet tutelage. Its leverage lies in political commissars inside the army, in student radicals and in Chinese support, making it the most dangerous rival to the northern officers around Ngouabi.

20.name: Les Fils du Pool
20.text:
In the Lari and Kongo south, resentment runs high against a regime of northern officers that ousted two southern presidents in five years. The Sons of the Pool is the name of this populist mood, embodied by Bernard Kolélas, detained after being accused of plotting against Ngouabi in 1969.

It appeals to southern pride, Christian faith and hostility to 'atheist' Marxism and northern domination, promising to return power to the majority of the south. Its leverage is numbers: the Pool and Brazzaville's southern quarters hold much of the population, and unrest there can paralyse the capital.

21.name: Le Commando Kinganga
21.text:
Lieutenant Pierre Kinganga, nicknamed 'Siroko', is a cashiered Congolese officer and fervent Youlouist who fled across the river to Kinshasa. There he trains a small armed band of exiles and deserters, determined to storm Brazzaville and destroy the 'red' regime by force.

The commando rejects politics in favour of armed action, combining fanatical anti-communism, Lari nationalism and a cult of violence. It has no programme beyond the overthrow of Ngouabi and the restoration of Youlou's order. Its leverage lies in surprise, Zairean tolerance and contacts among discontented soldiers inside Brazzaville.

22.name: Armée populaire nationale
22.text:
The Congolese army, reorganised as the People's National Army after the 1968 seizure of power, is the true master of the state. Its officers sat on the National Council of the Revolution, and its former paratroop commander Marien Ngouabi now leads both the country and the new party.

The army demands discipline, national unity and its own prerogatives above the quarrels of party ideologues and student radicals. It is armed and advised by the Soviet bloc, yet its officers remain jealous of their independence. No government in Brazzaville can survive without its loyalty, and every faction courts it.
22.wiki: Armed Forces of the Republic of the Congo

23.name: Royaume téké
23.text:
The Makoko, king of the Téké at Mbé on the Batéké plateaux, holds the oldest throne in Congo; it was his predecessor who signed the 1880 treaty with Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza that founded French rule. The kingship survives as a ritual and moral authority, respected but without formal power.

The royal court defends the dignity of the Téké, customary land rights and the role of chiefs in village life, and resents the revolutionary regime's contempt for 'feudal' institutions. Its leverage is symbolic, rooted in history and ritual that every Congolese government has found useful to honour.
